source.title: Double descent in quantum kernel methods
source.authors: Marie C. Kempkes; Aroosa Ijaz; Elies Gil-Fuster; Carlos Bravo-Prieto; Jakob Spiegelberg; E. V. van Nieuwenburg; V. Dunjko

record.tranche_reason: Tests double descent in quantum kernel methods, using linear regression and quantum feature maps rather than the original deep-network settings.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-error sweeps and ablations. It also discusses earlier studies, but those cited results are not recorded as rows. Training-error curves are omitted because the claim concerns test error.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own test-error sweeps over training-set size for ridgeless quantum kernel regression, on synthetic and real data. This is a new setting (quantum feature spaces) for sample-wise double descent. It also reports ablations of residual error and regularization that bear on the noise and regularization account.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that linear regression in quantum feature spaces (quantum kernel methods) exhibits a test-error peak at the interpolation threshold N=p, shown analytically (Marčenko–Pastur, asymptotic, Gaussian inputs) and numerically on synthetic and real data. They attribute the peak to small singular values, test-feature alignment and residual error. They note that practical benefit depends on a deeper second dip, which they do not establish.
record.recipe_differences: Uses linear regression in quantum feature spaces and ridgeless quantum kernel methods, with sample-size sweeps and random-matrix analysis; not the original deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The peak is affected by singular-value cutoffs, retained test-feature modes, residual error, regularization strength, finite-shot sampling noise, kernel type, dataset, and feature-space dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: Simulated finite-shot noise in Gram and test-kernel entries smooths the curve and reduces peak prominence (Fig. F.3, n=2, Fashion MNIST).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Measurement or estimation noise in kernel entries acts as implicit regularization that dampens the interpolation peak.

record.problems: The main curves are presented as figures without numerical values in the text. Empirical repetitions use five independently sampled training sets. The theorem relies on assumptions including Gaussian inputs and asymptotic limits, while the experiments are finite-scale; the paper notes that exact function evaluation avoids finite-shot approximation in its main analysis.
record.rows_left_out: Training-error curves in Appendix F, Fig. F.2 were left out because they are not test-error results. Other detailed ablation parameter curves in Fig. 3 and Fig. F.1 were not separately itemized; the reported residual-error ablation relevant to V6 is included in R7.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep of deep networks.
No epoch or training-time sweep; models are closed-form ridgeless regression.
Capacity is not varied at fixed data. Curves are test error vs N/p from N sweeps, and no classical U-shape is shown being subsumed.
Peak location is tied to feature dimension p (4^n or 3n+2). No single effective-complexity measure is tested across size, epochs and samples.
Label noise is not varied as such. Multiple or triple descent is not examined. Optimally tuned regularization is not identified.

missing.what: Residual-error ablation on real-world data. Text: eliminating residual error 'significantly reduces or removes' the peak.
missing.locator: Appendix F(a), Fig. F.1(c), Fashion MNIST and California Housing, n=3

missing.what: Singular-value cutoff (spectral truncation, a regularization-like operation) reduces the peak; smaller cutoffs give a more pronounced peak.
Peak location scales linearly with qubit number for RDM kernels vs exponentially for EQK, i.e. the peak sits at N=p as p changes.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. All evidence is figure-only, with five repetitions and 100 test points. The x-axis is N/p with p fixed by the feature map; that makes this sample-wise double descent, so V4 (capacity-wise) is not directly tested even though the model class is non-deep. The Section III decomposition is in-class (relative to the best linear model), not the classical bias–variance split.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over deep-network model size; varying training-set size or quantum feature dimension is not a test of model-wise double descent in deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The study tests sample-size sweeps in quantum kernel methods near the interpolation threshold, not other model classes or data regimes beyond those reported.
Tests quantum kernel linear-regression models; does not establish the curve across all model classes or characterize all classical U-shaped curves.
Does not test a single effective-complexity measure across model size, epochs, and sample size.
Tests a variance-like/residual-error contribution and reports regularization sweeps. It does not test label noise specifically, multiple or triple descent, or optimally tuned regularization.
Does not test whether an appropriate effective parameter count turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.operation_detail: Removed the residual-error contribution by using the underlying distribution in fitting.
rows.value: figure only; the text reports test error drops to zero at interpolation and in the underparameterized regime when residual error is eliminated
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over five independent experiment repetitions, each with independently sampled training data
rows.note: The authors identify the common error term as variance-like and say eliminating residual error removes the peak under these conditions.

rows.subject: QKMs using the EQK
rows.operation_detail: Varied the regularization parameter λ in a regularized kernel-method sweep.
rows.measure: Mean squared test error versus number of training data points
rows.value: figure only; the text states that increasing λ makes the peak less pronounced and eventually removes it
rows.note: Regularization values are shown in the figure; the text does not identify an optimally tuned value.
rows.check: State should be observed: the text says the peak 'becomes less pronounced and eventually disappears' as λ grows. Optimal tuning is untested, but that is a gap in coverage, not a weaker effect.

rows.measure: Mean squared test error versus number of training data points
rows.value: figure only; the text says shot noise smooths the curve and reduces the prominence of the peak
rows.note: This is sampling noise in kernel estimates, not a test of label noise.
rows.check: Finite-shot noise on kernel estimates is neither label noise nor explicit regularization. Authors only say it acts 'similarly to a regularization'. Move to fits_no_version.
